replacements.instruction: Compact Discussion by merging adjacent restatements while preserving the pointwise-versus-pairwise interpretation, system-level ablation interpretation, execution caveat, selective adaptivity comparison, benchmark-design implication, and cognitive-theory framing.
replacements.before:
Tables~\ref{tab:main-results} and~\ref{tab:pairwise-results} show that the clearest advantage of \condAgenticCogWriter\ is not uniform dominance under every pointwise score, but consistent preference in direct same-prompt comparisons.
The pattern supports process-level control as a useful way to organize long-form generation without requiring it to maximize every benchmark-specific metric.

Table~\ref{tab:ablation-results} suggests that the advantage is better interpreted at the system level than assigned to either explicit goals or adaptive ordering alone.
Removing the goal representation or fixing the process order leaves performance near the full system, whereas the larger \condSingleWriter\ gap points to execution structure as another candidate explanation.
The post-hoc \condSingleContext\ diagnostic, however, does not reduce that difference to subagent delegation alone.
The current evidence therefore supports the coordinated writing loop more strongly than any single tested mechanism.

Figure~\ref{fig:process-sequences} and Table~\ref{tab:process-dynamics} add a complementary view of adaptivity.
\condAgenticCogWriter\ usually follows planning--drafting--reviewing and departs from that path only selectively, so process-level control should not be equated with continual replanning.
This perspective complements systems that adapt task decomposition or structural reasoning during generation~\citep{xiong2025beyond,wan2025cognitive,sun2026cot}: another design axis is not only how dynamically a writer replans, but what kind of writing action its controller selects.

The process findings suggest a more targeted evaluation agenda for writing agents.
Long inputs and, where stated, long requested outputs, together with procedural constraints, make document production demanding but do not necessarily create reasons to revisit earlier decisions.
Future benchmarks could test process control directly by changing objectives, introducing new evidence, or imposing rhetorical constraints during composition.
More broadly, cognitive writing theory provides executable control abstractions rather than claiming that language agents reproduce human cognition: it makes alternative writing processes explicit enough to implement, compare, and falsify.
replacements.after:
Tables~\ref{tab:main-results} and~\ref{tab:pairwise-results} show that \condAgenticCogWriter\ is distinguished by consistent same-prompt preference rather than uniform pointwise dominance, supporting process-level control without requiring every benchmark-specific metric to peak.
Table~\ref{tab:ablation-results} further suggests a system-level interpretation: removing goals or fixing process order leaves performance near the full system, whereas the larger \condSingleWriter\ gap points to execution structure; the post-hoc \condSingleContext\ diagnostic does not isolate that gap to subagent delegation.
The evidence therefore supports the coordinated writing loop more strongly than any single tested mechanism.

Figure~\ref{fig:process-sequences} and Table~\ref{tab:process-dynamics} show that \condAgenticCogWriter\ usually follows planning--drafting--reviewing and departs selectively, so process-level control should not be equated with continual replanning.
This complements systems that adapt task decomposition or structural reasoning during generation~\citep{xiong2025beyond,wan2025cognitive,sun2026cot}: another design axis is what writing action a controller selects, not only how dynamically it replans.

These process findings motivate benchmarks that directly induce revision: long inputs and, where stated, long requested outputs, together with procedural constraints, can be demanding without requiring earlier decisions to be revisited.
Future benchmarks could change objectives, introduce new evidence, or impose rhetorical constraints during composition.
More broadly, cognitive writing theory provides executable control abstractions rather than claims that language agents reproduce human cognition, making alternative writing processes explicit enough to implement, compare, and falsify.

replacements.before:
\condAgenticCogWriter\ reframes long-form writing for AI agents as a process-level control problem.
A top-level \texttt{Monitor} chooses whether to plan, draft, or review from persistent writing state and delegates the selected process to a role-specific subagent.
Across three long-form writing benchmarks, our system is preferred to single-pass generation, fixed writing stages, and adaptive task planning in direct same-prompt comparisons.
Component analyses show that neither explicit goals nor adaptive process ordering alone accounts for the overall advantage, while process traces show that most runs follow a single planning--drafting--reviewing cycle.
Together, these results support process-level control as a promising design for long-form writing agents and show how cognitive writing theory can yield executable, falsifiable system hypotheses.
replacements.after:
\condAgenticCogWriter\ reframes long-form writing for AI agents as a process-level control problem: a top-level \texttt{Monitor} selects planning, drafting, or reviewing from persistent writing state and delegates each process to a role-specific subagent.
Across three long-form writing benchmarks, our system is preferred to single-pass generation, fixed writing stages, and adaptive task planning in direct same-prompt comparisons; component analyses show that neither explicit goals nor adaptive process ordering alone explains the advantage, while most traces follow a single planning--drafting--reviewing cycle.
Together, these results support process-level control as a promising design for long-form writing agents and show how cognitive writing theory can yield executable, falsifiable system hypotheses.
